In [[mathematical analysis]], '''Ekeland's variational principle''', discovered by [[Ivar Ekeland]],<ref name="Eke74">{{cite journal|doi=10.1016/0022-247X(74)90025-0|last=Ekeland|first=Ivar|author-link=Ivar Ekeland
|title= On the variational principle|journal=J. Math. Anal. Appl.|volume=47|year=1974|issue=2|pages=324–353|issn=0022-247X|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last=Ekeland|first=Ivar|title=Nonconvex minimization problems|journal=Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society|series=New Series|volume=1|year=1979|number=3|pages=443–474|doi=10.1090/S0273-0979-1979-14595-6|mr=526967|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last1=Ekeland|first1=Ivar|last2=Temam|first2=Roger|author2link=Roger Temam|title=Convex analysis and variational problems|edition=Corrected reprinting of the (1976) North-Holland|series=Classics in applied mathematics|volume=28 |publisher=Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics&nbsp;(SIAM)|location=Philadelphia,&nbsp;PA|year=1999|pages=357–373|isbn=0-89871-450-8|mr=1727362}}</ref> is a theorem that asserts that there exist nearly optimal solutions to some [[optimization problem]]s.

Ekeland's principle can be used when the lower [[level set]] of a minimization problems is not [[Compactness (topology)|compact]], so that the [[Bolzano&ndash;Weierstrass theorem]] cannot be applied. The principle relies on the [[Complete metric space|completeness]] of the [[metric space]].<ref name="KG90"/>

The principle has been shown to be equivalent to completeness of metric spaces.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Sullivan|first=Francis|title=A characterization of complete metric spaces|journal=Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society|volume=83|number=2|date=October 1981|pages=345–346|doi=10.1090/S0002-9939-1981-0624927-9|mr=624927|doi-access=free}}</ref>
In [[proof theory]], it is equivalent to [[Reverse_mathematics#Π11_comprehension_Π11-CA0|Π{{su|p=1|b=1}}CA<sub>0</sub> over RCA<sub>0</sub>]], i.e. relatively strong.

It also leads to a quick proof of the [[Caristi fixed point theorem]].<ref name="KG90">{{cite book|last1=Kirk|first1=William A.|first2=Kazimierz|last2=Goebel|title=Topics in Metric Fixed Point Theory|year=1990|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=0-521-38289-0}}</ref><ref name="realanalysisok">{{cite book|last=Ok|first=Efe|title=Real Analysis with Economic Applications|publisher=Princeton University Press|year=2007|pages=664|chapter=D: Continuity I|isbn=978-0-691-11768-3|url=http://homepages.nyu.edu/~eo1/Book-PDF/Ekeland.pdf|access-date=January 31, 2009}}</ref>

==History==

Ekeland was associated with the [[Paris Dauphine University]] when he proposed this theorem.<ref name="Eke74"/>

==Ekeland's variational principle==

===Preliminary definitions===

A function <math>f : X \to \R \cup \{-\infty, +\infty\}</math> valued in the [[extended real numbers]] <math>\R \cup \{-\infty, +\infty\} = [-\infty, +\infty]</math> is said to be '''{{em|{{visible anchor|bounded below}}}}''' if <math>\inf_{} f(X) = \inf_{x \in X} f(x) > -\infty</math> and it is called '''{{em|[[Proper convex function|{{visible anchor|proper map|text=proper}}]]}}''' if it has a non-empty '''{{em|[[effective domain|{{visible anchor|effective domain}}]]}}''', which by definition is the set 
<math display=block>\operatorname{dom} f ~\stackrel{\scriptscriptstyle\text{def}}{=}~ \{x \in X : f(x) \neq +\infty\},</math>
and it is never equal to <math>-\infty.</math> In other words, a map is {{em|proper}} if is valued in <math>\R \cup \{+\infty\}</math> and not identically <math>+\infty.</math> 
The map <math>f</math> is proper and bounded below if and only if <math>-\infty < \inf_{} f(X) \neq +\infty,</math> or equivalently, if and only if <math>\inf_{} f(X) \in \R.</math>

A function <math>f :X \to  [-\infty, +\infty]</math> is {{em|[[lower semicontinuous]]}} at a given <math>x_0 \in X</math> if for every real <math>y < f\left(x_0\right)</math> there exists a [[Neighborhood (topology)|neighborhood]] <math>U</math> of <math>x_0</math> such that <math>f(u) > y</math> for all <math>u \in U.</math> 
A function is called {{em|[[lower semicontinuous]]}} if it is lower semicontinuous at every point of <math>X,</math> which happens if and only if <math>\{x \in X : ~f(x) > y\}</math> is an [[open set]] for every <math>y \in \R,</math> or equivalently, if and only if all of its lower [[level set]]s <math>\{x \in X : ~f(x) \leq y\}</math> are [[Closed set|closed]]. 

===Statement of the theorem===

{{Math theorem
|name = {{visible anchor|EVP|text=Ekeland's variational principle}}{{sfn|Zalinescu|2002|p=29}} 
|math_statement =
Let <math>(X, d)</math> be a [[complete metric space]] and let <math>f : X \to \R \cup \{+\infty\}</math> be a [[#proper map|proper]] [[lower semicontinuous]] function that is [[#bounded below|bounded below]] (so <math>\inf_{} f(X) \in \R</math>). 
Pick <math>x_0 \in X</math> such that <math>f(x_0) \in \R</math> (or equivalently, <math>f(x_0) \neq +\infty</math>) and fix any real <math>\varepsilon > 0.</math> 
There exists some <math>v \in X</math> such that 
<math display=block>f(v) ~\leq~ f\left(x_0\right) - \varepsilon \; d \left(x_0, v\right)</math> 
and for every <math>x \in X</math> other than <math>v</math> (that is, <math>x \neq v</math>),
<math display=block>f(v) ~<~ f(x) + \varepsilon \; d(v, x).</math>
}}

{{math proof | proof =
Define a function <math>G : X \times X \to \R \cup \{+\infty\}</math> by 
<math display=block>G(x, y) ~\stackrel{\scriptscriptstyle\text{def}}{=}~ f(x) + \varepsilon \; d(x, y)</math> 
which is lower semicontinuous because it is the sum of the lower semicontinuous function <math>f</math> and the continuous function <math>(x, y) \mapsto \varepsilon \; d(x, y).</math>
Given <math>z \in X,</math> denote the functions with one coordinate fixed at <math>z</math> by
<math display=block>G_z ~\stackrel{\scriptscriptstyle\text{def}}{=}~ G(z, \cdot) : X \to \R \cup \{+\infty\} \; \text{ and }</math> 
<math display=block>G^z~ \stackrel{\scriptscriptstyle\text{def}}{=}~ G(\cdot, z) : X \to \R \cup \{+\infty\}</math> 
and define the set
<math display=block>F(z) ~\stackrel{\scriptscriptstyle\text{def}}{=}~ \left\{y \in X : G^z(y) \leq f(z)\right\} ~=~ \{y \in X : f(y) + \varepsilon \; d(y, z) \leq f(z)\},</math>
which is not empty since <math>z \in F(z).</math> 
An element <math>v \in X</math> satisfies the conclusion of this theorem if and only if <math>F(v) = \{v\}.</math> It remains to find such an element.

It may be verified that for every <math>x \in X,</math>
# <math>F(x)</math> is closed (because <math>G^x \,\stackrel{\scriptscriptstyle\text{def}}{=}\, G(\cdot,x) : X \to \R \cup \{+\infty\}</math> is lower semicontinuous); 
# if <math>x \notin \operatorname{dom} f</math> then <math>F(x) = X;</math> 
# if <math>x \in \operatorname{dom} f</math> then <math>x \in F(x) \subseteq \operatorname{dom} f;</math> in particular, <math>x_0 \in F\left(x_0\right) \subseteq \operatorname{dom} f;</math>
# if <math>y \in F(x)</math> then <math>F(y) \subseteq F(x).</math> 

Let <math>s_0 = \inf_{x \in F\left(x_0\right)} f(x),</math> which is a real number because <math>f</math> was assumed to be bounded below. 
Pick <math>x_1 \in F\left(x_0\right)</math> such that <math>f\left(x_1\right) < s_0 + 2^{-1}.</math> 
Having defined <math>s_{n-1}</math> and <math>x_n,</math> let 
<math display=block>s_n ~\stackrel{\scriptscriptstyle\text{def}}{=}~ \inf_{x \in F\left(x_n\right)} f(x)</math>
and pick 
<math>x_{n+1} \in F\left(x_n\right)</math> 
such that 
<math>f\left(x_{n+1}\right) < s_n + 2^{-(n+1)}.</math> 
For any <math>n \geq 0,</math> <math>x_{n+1} \in F\left(x_n\right)</math> guarantees that <math>s_n \leq f\left(x_{n+1}\right)</math> and <math>F\left(x_{n+1}\right) \subseteq F\left(x_n\right),</math> which in turn implies <math>s_{n+1} \geq s_n</math> and thus also 
<math display=block>f\left(x_{n+2}\right) \geq s_{n+1} \geq s_n.</math> 
So if <math>n \geq 1</math> then <math>x_{n+1} \in F\left(x_n\right) \stackrel{\scriptscriptstyle\text{def}}{=} \left\{y \in X : f(y) + \varepsilon \; d\left(y, x_n\right) \leq f\left(x_n\right)\right\}</math> and <math>f\left(x_{n+1}\right) \geq s_{n-1},</math> which guarantee 
<math display=block>\varepsilon \; d\left(x_{n+1}, x_n\right) ~\leq~ f\left(x_n\right) - f\left(x_{n+1}\right) ~\leq~ f\left(x_n\right) - s_{n-1} ~<~ \frac{1}{2^n}.</math>

It follows that for all positive integers <math>n, p \geq 1,</math> 
<math display=block>d\left(x_{n+p}, x_n\right) ~\leq~ 2 \; \frac{\varepsilon^{-1}}{2^n},</math> 
which proves that <math>x_\bull := \left(x_n\right)_{n=0}^\infty</math> is a Cauchy sequence. 
Because <math>X</math> is a complete metric space, there exists some <math>v \in X</math> such that <math>x_\bull</math> converges to <math>v.</math> 
For any <math>n \geq 0,</math> since <math>F\left(x_n\right)</math> is a closed set that contain the sequence <math>x_n, x_{n+1}, x_{n+2}, \ldots,</math> it must also contain this sequence's limit, which is <math>v;</math> thus <math>v \in F\left(x_n\right)</math> and in particular, <math>v \in F\left(x_0\right).</math> 

The theorem will follow once it is shown that <math>F(v) = \{v\}.</math> 
So let <math>x \in F(v)</math> and it remains to show <math>x = v.</math> 
Because <math>x \in F\left(x_n\right)</math> for all <math>n \geq 0,</math> it follows as above that <math>\varepsilon \; d\left(x, x_n\right) \leq 2^{-n},</math> which implies that <math>x_{\bull}</math> converges to <math>x.</math> 
Because <math>x_\bull</math> also converges to <math>v</math> and limits in metric spaces are unique, <math>x = v.</math> <math>\blacksquare</math> [[Q.E.D.]]
}}

For example, if <math>f</math> and <math>(X, d)</math> are as in the theorem's statement and if <math>x_0 \in X</math> happens to be a global minimum point of <math>f,</math> then the vector <math>v</math> from the theorem's conclusion is <math>v := x_0.</math>

===Corollaries===

{{Math theorem
| name = Corollary{{sfn|Zalinescu|2002|p=30}} 
| math_statement =
Let <math>(X, d)</math> be a [[complete metric space]], and let <math>f : X \to \R \cup \{+\infty\}</math> be a [[lower semicontinuous]] functional on <math>X</math> that is bounded below and not identically equal to <math>+\infty.</math> Fix <math>\varepsilon > 0</math> and a point <math>x_0 \in X</math> such that
<math display=block>f\left(x_0\right) ~\leq~ \varepsilon + \inf_{x \in X} f(x).</math>
Then, for every <math>\lambda > 0,</math> there exists a point <math>v \in X</math> such that
<math display=block>f(v) ~\leq~ f\left(x_0\right),</math>
<math display=block>d\left(x_0, v\right) ~\leq~ \lambda,</math>
and, for all <math>x \neq v,</math>
<math display=block>f(x)+ \frac{\varepsilon}{\lambda} d(v, x) ~>~ f(v) .</math>
}}
The principle could be thought of as follows: For any point <math>x_0</math> which nearly realizes the infimum, there exists another point <math>v</math>, which is at least as good as <math>x_0</math>, it is close to <math>x_0</math> and the perturbed function, <math>f(x)+\frac{\varepsilon}{\lambda} d(v, x)</math>, has unique minimum at <math>v</math>. 
A good compromise is to take <math>\lambda := \sqrt{\varepsilon}</math> in the preceding result.{{sfn|Zalinescu|2002|p=30}}
